title: Confessions of a Rule Book Junkie
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W6U3fBgQoVg

Daniel (@dungeondive) finally works out *why* he cares so much about rulebooks, and the answer is 1980s video game manuals. On the Atari 2600 and the NES, the manual carried what the cartridge couldn't: the story, the bestiary, the real character art the sprites could only gesture at. Zelda and Metroid shipped 50-page books; Final Fantasy's Explorer's Handbook ran to 90. Almost everything known about Metroid's world came from that manual. He and his friends carried them in backpacks — no phones, so the manual was the only way to be with a game while away from it — and traded secrets from them on the playground. He still keeps a new rulebook in his bag, which is why portable size matters to him.

He's clear about what he isn't asking for: not perfection. Typos happen, edge cases surface, errata is necessary. What he wants is evidence of attention — art, theme, background, worked examples — because a publisher who cares about the documentation is one he can trust with the whole experience.

The back half tours ten rulebooks he admires: the Arkham Horror deluxe book (bought at full retail purely to get it, opening with a history of the game by Richard Launius); Dungeon Degenerates; Hellboy and Mantic's backpack-friendly comic-book format; Fallen Land's exhaustive examples; Kingdom Death: Monster; Shadows of Brimstone's adventure books; Shadows of Malice; Warhammer Quest Shadows Over Hammerhal and its 40-page novella; Silver Tower; Space Hulk; and the 1995 original. Along the way: credit your artists, and include an index.

----

Which rulebook do you actually enjoy reading — and does a well-made one raise your confidence in the game before a single piece hits the table?
